content: Detection of critical congenital heart defects (CCHDs) in newborns before the occurrence of acute cardiovascular collapse significantly improves health outcomes. Prenatal ultrasonography and postnatal clinical examination are the primary methods used for identifying these conditions. However, despite the availability of these methods, a substantial number of cases remain undetected. Pulse oximetry has been proposed as an additional screening tool to enhance the detection of CCHDs. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of pulse oximetry as a screening method for identifying CCHDs in asymptomatic newborns. The study also aimed to assess potential factors contributing to variability in results, such as whether antenatally detected congenital heart defects were included or excluded, the timing of the test (before or after 24 hours of life), the site of testing (pre-ductal and post-ductal versus post-ductal only), the type of oxygen saturation measurement (functional versus fractional), the study design (retrospective versus prospective), and the risk of bias in the flow and timing domain of the QUADAS-2 tool. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and HSRProj, up to March 2017. They also reviewed reference lists of included studies and relevant systematic reviews to identify additional studies. No language restrictions were applied. Studies were included if they met predefined criteria for design, population, tests, and outcomes. Both cross-sectional and cohort studies assessing the diagnostic accuracy of pulse oximetry in term and late preterm asymptomatic newborns were considered. Various pulse oximetry protocols were included, such as different oxygen saturation thresholds, pre-ductal and post-ductal measurements, and testing performed at different times after birth. Diagnostic echocardiography and clinical follow-up, including postmortem findings and congenital anomaly databases, served as the reference standards. Data on diagnostic accuracy were extracted from the included studies, and variability between studies was visually assessed using forest and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) plots. The risk of bias was evaluated using the QUADAS-2 tool. A bivariate model was used to calculate pooled sensitivity and specificity values, and subgroup analyses and meta-regression were performed to investigate sources of heterogeneity. A total of 21 studies, involving 457,202 participants, met the inclusion criteria. Nineteen studies, with 436,758 participants, provided data for the primary analysis, which used an oxygen saturation threshold of <95% or ≤95%. The overall sensitivity of pulse oximetry for detecting CCHD was 76.3% (95% confidence interval [CI] 69.5% to 82.0%), with low certainty of evidence. The specificity was 99.9% (95% CI 99.7% to 99.9%), with a high certainty of evidence. The false-positive rate was 0.14% (95% CI 0.07% to 0.22%). The summary positive likelihood ratio was 535.6 (95% CI 280.3 to 1023.4), and the negative likelihood ratio was 0.24 (95% CI 0.18 to 0.31). Based on these findings, for every 10,000 apparently healthy late preterm or full-term newborns, six are expected to have CCHD (median prevalence in the review). Pulse oximetry screening would correctly identify five of these infants as having CCHD, while one case would be missed. Additionally, 14 infants out of 10,000 would be falsely identified as having suspected CCHD when they do not actually have the condition. The false-positive rate was significantly lower when pulse oximetry was performed more than 24 hours after birth compared to within the first 24 hours (0.06%, 95% CI 0.03% to 0.13%, versus 0.42%, 95% CI 0.20% to 0.89%; P = 0.027). Forest and ROC plots revealed greater variability in sensitivity estimates compared to specificity across studies. Subgroup analyses and meta-regression were conducted to explore potential sources of heterogeneity, including the inclusion or exclusion of antenatally detected congenital heart defects, timing of testing, and risk of bias in the flow and timing domain of QUADAS-2. However, no clear explanation for the variability in sensitivity was identified. In conclusion, pulse oximetry is a highly specific and moderately sensitive screening tool for detecting CCHD in asymptomatic newborns, with very low false-positive rates. The current evidence supports the routine use of pulse oximetry screening for CCHD in newborns prior to discharge from the well-baby nursery.
